horoscopes.intro: November 16 in the stars: Find out what’s in store for you today in our daily horoscopes for Monday November 16. Read the daily horoscopes for your Sun sign or rising sign (ascendant) to plan your day.

aries.text: Feeling braver than usual this Monday, Aries? The skies are more than happy to support your courageous moves. Action planet Mars meets up with expansive Jupiter in your fifth house of romance, taking a connection from mild to muy picante. Scrap the Victorian playbook and make the first move. Subtle? Not today. Both planets can make you come on strong, though, so warm things up slowly instead of pouncing. This is also a stellar day for creative projects. Post your latest work or pitch an idea you’ve been sitting on. Someone influential could take notice. Already attached? Plan something for tonight that neither of you would call typical.

taurus.text: Anyone who crosses your people today will meet a wall, Taurus. Mars and abundant Jupiter meet in your fourth house of family, putting you in full defense mode, and that protectiveness extends to your own work as well. The catch is that you may not stop to check who’s actually attacking. Before you bare your fangs, consider the source, since a dear friend or relative could be handing you sound advice in a clumsy wrapper.

gemini.text: People will hang on your every word today, Gemini, so choose them wisely. Feisty Mars joins jovial Jupiter in your third house of communication, making you a compelling presence in any room or thread. Use your voice to speak up for a cause and you could raise awareness, maybe even some money. That same firepower works in an argument, though, and no one is likely to outtalk you. Pull your punches if a conversation gets too heated. The snappiest comeback of the day can still do lasting damage to a relationship you’d rather keep.

cancer.text: Guard those purse strings today, Cancer. Money burns a hole in your pocket with impulsive Mars and indulgent Jupiter aligned in your luxuriating second house, leaving you helpless in the face of pretty, shiny things. Do you need it, or do you simply want it very badly at 2PM on a Monday? Start a Pinterest board or a Black Friday wish list instead of buying on impulse. The sales are still three weeks out, so nothing is getting away from you. And if you can’t resist, save the receipt, because this might be one worth returning.

leo.text: You’ve got no filter today, Leo, and you may not want one. Brash Mars syncs up with bloviating Jupiter in your sign, making you irrepressibly candid. You’re simply speaking with passion, though others could read it as confrontation. Is a little pushiness ever warranted? Absolutely. If someone needs a nudge to get moving, don’t back down from your stance. You know it’ll benefit them in the end. Save the full roar for something that deserves it, like a matter you’re fully invested in.

virgo.text: Deep breaths, Virgo. Today’s Mars-Jupiter meetup in your shadowy twelfth house could magnify your worries, so don’t let them send you into a tailspin. Is the situation as dire as the version playing in your head? This is the day to lean on a logical friend who can help you untangle it. This planetary pairing can also stir up old wounds. Healing is a process, so if you need to talk about the hurt again, there’s no shame in it. Pick the friends who won’t tell you to “get over it already.”

libra.text: Friction in the comments section! Today’s scrappy Mars-Jupiter meetup in your teamwork zone makes collaboration both electric and exasperating. With the right people, you’ll feel real possibility, so gather a few of them for a think-tank session and see what shakes out. As for the organizations falling apart at the seams, why stick around? You don’t have to take one for the team, and you never signed up for that role anyway. Opt out today, or give yourself plenty of room so you don’t absorb anyone else’s drama.

scorpio.text: A career quest picks up speed this Monday, Scorpio. Mars meets Jupiter in your ambitious tenth house, so tap into your drive and take action while the week is young. Pushing people a little is fine. Strong-arming them, on the other hand? That’s where things unravel. The downside of this pairing is that its energy can go from motivating to aggressive without much warning. You could win the battle by sheer force and start a cold war in the process. Make the ask, then give people room to say yes on their own schedule.

sagittarius.text: Bigger, stronger, faster! Today’s Mars-Jupiter meetup in your ninth house sounds the call for expansion, and with your ruler involved, you won’t need much convincing. Without risk there’s no reward, Sag. Read the directions and get the lay of the land first, but accept that you’ll make a few mistakes as you stretch and grow. Chalk them up as learning experiences. You’ll never collect any unless you try something new.

capricorn.text: Lust be a Sea Goat tonight! Frisky Mars syncs up with bawdy Jupiter in your seductive eighth house and you’re running hot. The cat-and-mouse routine has been fun, but your patience is wearing thin. How much longer do you plan to hedge before making your desires known? The time has come for your reveal, or at least to be considerably more obvious than you’ve managed so far. The same goes for a business dealing. Put the offer on the table and let them react to a real number instead of a hint.

aquarius.text: Is it getting a little too hot in that kitchen, Aquarius? Today’s Mars-Jupiter merger turns up the flame on your relationships, and you may realize a partnership is moving faster than you’d like. Before you head for the door, make sure you aren’t operating on assumptions. Have you actually asked what the other person expects of you? If they’re reasonable, there should be plenty of room to negotiate, and you might discover the pace is moving along just fine.

pisces.text: Today’s Mars-Jupiter merger could turn you into a raging perfectionist, so stay on high alert. You could fuss over something until midnight, Pisces, only to find another “flaw.” While you like things done just so, think twice if that means losing a night’s sleep or blowing your budget. Who exactly are you trying to impress here? Push too hard and you may wind up intimidating them, or leaving them feeling like they could never measure up. Finish it, send it, and go to bed at a reasonable hour.

items.title: Brain health in children born extremely preterm: a multidimensional perspective
items.originalTitle: Brain health in children born extremely preterm: a multidimensional perspective
items.summary: Gestational age and developmental stage of the brain at birth are major determinants of child health, and long-term consequences of preterm birth and altered brain maturation are inadequately understood simply through brain injury, survival rates, or diagnostic labels.
items.caution: A link, not proof of cause.
items.abstract: Gestational age and developmental stage of the brain at birth are major determinants of child health, and long-term consequences of preterm birth and altered brain maturation are inadequately understood simply through brain injury, survival rates, or diagnostic labels. In this Review, we conceptualise brain health in children born extremely preterm (before 28 weeks' gestation) as a developmental condition shaped by maturational timing, biological vulnerability, neonatal intensive care exposure, sensory and relational experiences, family circumstances, and social environments. We integrate evidence from research on early brain development and consciousness, long-term multidomain neurodevelopmental outcomes, neonatal intensive care practice, relational caregiving, early developmental interventions, and ethical, psychological, and social dimensions of care. Across these domains, extremely preterm birth emerges not as a single event but as a neuroplastic system that adapts to biological and environmental risks and protective factors that shape neurodevelopmental resilience and vulnerabilities and establish developmental trajectories. We argue that care for the infant born extremely preterm is optimised through a brain-health framework where care becomes a longitudinal, ethical process that integrates family support, minimises harmful exposures, promotes adaptive development, and fosters participation, wellbeing, and quality of life.

items.title: Exposure to violence in public places in the country of resettlement and its associations with psychosocial well-being and mental health among children and young adults with refugee backgrounds: a systematic review
items.originalTitle: Exposure to violence in public places in the country of resettlement and its associations with psychosocial well-being and mental health among children and young adults with refugee backgrounds: a systematic review
items.summary: Children and young adults with refugee backgrounds face various forms of adversity during migration.
items.caution: Strongest kind of evidence — still check who took part.
items.abstract: Children and young adults with refugee backgrounds face various forms of adversity during migration. To facilitate synthesis of this literature, violence in public places (ViPP) was conceptualised as an analytical umbrella framework encompassing different forms of intentional violence occurring in public or community settings, including direct victimisation, witnessing violence, or hearing about violence experienced by others. This review synthesises evidence on the prevalence and forms of such exposure and its associations with psychosocial well-being and mental health among children and young adults with refugee backgrounds. Eight databases (ERIC, PubMed, PsycINFO, Scopus, Web of Science, EconLit, Google Scholar and CINAHL) and 16 grey literature sources were systematically searched for quantitative studies published up to May 2025. Eligible studies included participants with refugee backgrounds, had a mean study population age of ≤ 24 years, reported quantitative data on violence exposure in public or community settings corresponding to the ViPP framework, and assessed psychosocial well-being and/or mental health outcomes. Quality appraisal was performed using the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) critical appraisal tool and findings were synthesised narratively. Seven studies were included from 15,109 screened articles, comprising 759 participants with refugee backgrounds who were forcibly displaced from six geographical regions. All included studies examined violence exposures in countries of resettlement among refugee populations who had experienced cross-border displacement. Violence exposures corresponding to the ViPP framework were common, particularly indirect victimisation and witnessing violence, with prevalence ranging from 19% to 66%. Higher levels of violence exposure were associated with poorer psychosocial and mental health outcomes, although findings were heterogeneous, and evidence on specific forms of violence and subgroup differences was limited. The findings indicate that violence exposure may continue after resettlement and highlight violence exposure in public and community settings as an under-recognised post-migration risk. The ViPP framework may facilitate a broader understanding of violence occurring in public and community settings among refugee populations after resettlement.

items.title: Interventions to reduce perinatal suicidality: a global systematic review
items.originalTitle: Interventions to reduce perinatal suicidality: a global systematic review

items.source: Journal of reproductive and infant psychology
items.abstract:
Introduction: Perinatal suicidality (suicidal thoughts, behaviours, plans and attempts) is a risk factor for suicide. Evidence on interventions to reduce perinatal suicidality remains limited. This systematic review examined the effectiveness of non-pharmacological interventions to reduce suicidality in perinatal women.

Methods: This review was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251081528). Seven databases were searched from 2010 to December 2025. Interventions assessing a reduction in perinatal suicidality as a primary, secondary, or safety monitoring outcome were included. Two reviewers independently screened articles. A narrative summary was compiled. Risk of bias was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool.

Results: Six studies were included: 5 randomised controlled trials (3 individually randomised, 1 cluster, 1 noninferiority) and 1 historical controlled trial. Three studies investigated suicidality as a primary or secondary outcome, and three studies collected suicidality data for safety monitoring. Of these, two investigated multidisciplinary community health programmes, and one evaluated a behavioural activation therapy. Two studies showed a reduction in suicidality, and one showed a significant reduction at 3-4 months postpartum, but not at 7-8 months. Three studies assessed suicidality as safety monitoring. These studies investigated eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing therapy, a practice-level intervention incorporated into obstetric practices, and an electronic mindfulness-based intervention. These studies were not adequately powered to assess a reduction in suicidality.

Discussion: Few studies have investigated suicidality as a primary or secondary outcome. Although some health system level and psychological interventions were associated with a reduction in suicidality, robust evidence from interventions specifically designed to reduce perinatal suicidality is needed.

items.abstract: Background/Objectives: The world is undergoing rapid population aging while experiencing more frequent and intense heatwaves driven by climate change. People living with dementia-who can have impaired thermoregulation, a reduced ability to perceive and respond to heat, and high care dependency-may be especially susceptible to heat, but the evidence on mortality has not been synthesized. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to quantify the association between heatwave exposure and dementia-related mortality. Methods: PubMed, Web of Science Core Collection, ProQuest Dissertations & Theses Global, and APA PsycINFO were searched from inception to 15 June 2026; the searches were rerun on 15 October 2026 and supplemented by citation searching and by a PubMed search without the older-adult concept block. The review is reported according to PRISMA 2020 (PROSPERO CRD420261436457, registered after the searches had been run). Observational studies reporting relative effect estimates for mortality during defined heatwave or extreme heat events, among people with diagnosed dementia or for deaths attributed to dementia in mortality records, were eligible. Risk of bias was assessed with an adapted ROBINS-E approach and the certainty of evidence with GRADE. Odds ratios (ORs) from time-stratified case-crossover analyses, which estimate rate ratios, were pooled in a random-effects model with restricted maximum-likelihood estimation and Hartung-Knapp 95% confidence intervals (CIs); heterogeneity was described with Cochran's Q, I2, and a 95% prediction interval. The primary analysis was restricted to studies with a dementia-specific outcome definition and an estimate of the total heatwave association and used one study from each pair of studies based on the same mortality data. Results: Six studies conducted in China and Australia met the eligibility criteria, one of them identified only by the supplementary search; three contributed to the primary analysis, and three were used in sensitivity analyses only. All study-level estimates exceeded unity, but the pooled association was imprecise and not statistically significant (OR 1.84, 95% CI 0.54-6.25), with high heterogeneity (I2 = 94.9%; 95% prediction interval 0.21-16.31). items.title: Current state of dementia screening, risk reduction strategies, and barriers to the uptake of evidence-based dementia care in primary healthcare in Africa: a scoping review and call for implementation research

items.abstract:
Introduction: Dementia is a growing public health challenge worldwide, particularly in Africa. Although various screening tools have been used across different settings in the region, evidence on dementia screening practices, risk reduction strategies, and barriers to evidence-based dementia care has not been systematically mapped. This scoping review aimed to map the available evidence on dementia screening practices, risk reduction approaches, and barriers to dementia care across Africa.

Methods: This scoping review was conducted in accordance with the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology for scoping reviews and reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines. The review protocol was prospectively registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF). A comprehensive search of major databases (PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, Google Scholar) and grey literature was conducted. Eligible studies focused on dementia screening, risk reduction strategies, and barriers to evidence-based dementia care in primary healthcare settings across Africa. Study selection and data extraction were independently performed by three reviewers, and findings were synthesized using descriptive mapping.

Results: Of the 3,102 records identified, 16 studies met the inclusion criteria. Nine studies reported dementia screening practices using a range of screening tools, most commonly the Brief Community Screening Instrument for Dementia (CSID) and the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE). The available evidence suggests that dementia screening was largely conducted within research settings rather than as part of routine primary healthcare. Six studies identified barriers to evidence-based dementia screening and care, including workforce shortages, limited infrastructure and funding, inadequate training, low policy prioritization, sociocultural stigma, and limited public awareness. Only one study evaluated the implementation of dementia risk reduction strategies in an African context, highlighting an important evidence gap.

Conclusions: Evidence on dementia screening, risk reduction, and care integration in African primary healthcare remains limited. Key barriers include health system constraints, workforce shortages, inadequate infrastructure and funding, and sociocultural challenges. Future implementation research should evaluate culturally appropriate strategies

items.title: Acute Care Utilization and Cost Outcomes of Home-Based Palliative Care for Persons Living with Dementia in the United States: A Systematic Review
items.originalTitle: Acute Care Utilization and Cost Outcomes of Home-Based Palliative Care for Persons Living with Dementia in the United States: A Systematic Review
items.summary: Given the shift toward value-based payment models, which reward high-quality and cost-effective care, an increasing number of palliative care programs are being integrated across care settings in health systems and organizations in the United States to reduce patient use of more costly services such as hospitalization and emergency department (ED) visits.

items.abstract:
Background: Given the shift toward value-based payment models, which reward high-quality and cost-effective care, an increasing number of palliative care programs are being integrated across care settings in health systems and organizations in the United States to reduce patient use of more costly services such as hospitalization and emergency department (ED) visits. Home-based palliative care (HBPalC) is one community-based palliative care delivery model that may help delay facility and nursing home placement and reduce hospital use and costs.

Objective: This review synthesized evidence on hospital utilization and cost outcomes associated with HBPalC among people living with dementia (PLWD) in the United States.

Method: PubMed, Embase, and Cumulated Index in Nursing and Allied Health Literature were searched from inception through October 2025. All U.S.-based studies were included if samples included PLWD and the study examined the impact of HBPalC on hospital utilization (i.e., hospitalization and ED use) or health care costs.

Results: A total of eight studies were included. Overall, HBPalC provided core services such as symptom management and advanced care planning. PLWD-specific HBPalC focused on addressing neurobehavioral symptoms and supporting caregivers. HBPalC was consistently associated with reductions in hospitalization and associated costs, although evidence for changes in ED utilization was not available, with no studies reporting ED outcomes for PLWD specifically.

Conclusion: HBPalC was associated with reduced hospitalization, but its impact on ED use was inconclusive for PLWD. Most studies had heterogeneous patient samples and did not report PLWD-specific outcomes. There is a lack of HBPalC specifically designed for PLWD, and more studies are needed to evaluate HBPalC's impact on ED use among PLWD.

items.title: Effects of exercise training on the severity of sleep disorders and mental health outcomes in patients with obstructive sleep apnea and insomnia: A systematic review
items.originalTitle: Effects of exercise training on the severity of sleep disorders and mental health outcomes in patients with obstructive sleep apnea and insomnia: A systematic review
items.summary: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a chronic respiratory disorder characterized by recurrent upper airway collapse, associated with increased cardiometabolic risk and symptoms of depression and anxiety, whereas insomnia is characterized by persistent sleep difficulties and emotional and cognitive impairments.
items.caution: Strongest kind of evidence — still check who took part.
items.abstract:
Introduction: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a chronic respiratory disorder characterized by recurrent upper airway collapse, associated with increased cardiometabolic risk and symptoms of depression and anxiety, whereas insomnia is characterized by persistent sleep difficulties and emotional and cognitive impairments.

Objective: To analyze the available scientific evidence on the effects of different physical training protocols on mental health outcomes, particularly symptoms of depression and anxiety, in individuals with OSA and/or insomnia.

Methods: A systematic review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. Randomized controlled trials that investigated physical training interventions in adults with OSA and/or insomnia and assessed mental health outcomes were included. Searches were performed in PubMed, Cochrane Library, ScienceDirect, Scopus, and LILACS databases.

Results: Of the 535 studies initially identified, five randomized controlled trials met the eligibility criteria, totaling 187 participants, predominantly sedentary adults and older adults. Three studies investigated individuals with OSA and two involved populations with insomnia. Intervention protocols were mainly based on structured aerobic exercise, particularly walking, performed at least three times per week at moderate to vigorous intensity. The studies reported significant reductions in symptoms of depression, anxiety, and fatigue, as well as improvements in sleep quality and daytime sleepiness.

Conclusion: Regular aerobic exercise yields clinically relevant improvements in mental health and sleep outcomes in individuals with OSA and insomnia; however, the evidence remains limited by the low number of randomized trials, heterogeneous protocols, and small sample sizes.

items.title: Tracing Responses to a Syndemic: A Systematic Map of Substance Use, Mental and Sexual Health Interventions for Gay, Bisexual and Other Men Who Have Sex With Men in Southeast Asia
items.originalTitle: Tracing Responses to a Syndemic: A Systematic Map of Substance Use, Mental and Sexual Health Interventions for Gay, Bisexual and Other Men Who Have Sex With Men in Southeast Asia
items.summary: In Southeast Asia, a triple syndemic of substance use, poor mental and sexual health is shaped by regional political, economic and sociocultural environments and disproportionately affects gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (GBMSM).

items.abstract:
Introduction: In Southeast Asia, a triple syndemic of substance use, poor mental and sexual health is shaped by regional political, economic and sociocultural environments and disproportionately affects gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (GBMSM). Yet, most GBMSM implementation research, regionally and globally, focuses narrowly on HIV prevention and care, with little attention to mental health and substance use. This review aimed to systematically map interventions addressing these interlinked areas of GBMSM wellbeing in Southeast Asia, identify evidence gaps and inform the design of holistic, syndemic-responsive interventions.

Methods: Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, we searched six databases (01/2010-06/2024) for intervention/evaluation studies including GBMSM (cis and trans) in Southeast Asia, reporting outcomes on substance use, mental and/or sexual health. We completed citation/full text screening and data extraction in duplicate. We mapped interventions by type and availability of outcome data.

Results: We identified 2016 unique records; 142 publications reported 130 studies describing 148 interventions reaching 154,502 GBMSM. Interventions focused primarily on sexual health (n = 143), concentrated along the care continuum. This included facility-based HIV testing (n = 25), community-based HIV testing (n = 14), HIV self-testing (n = 13), assisted partner notification (n = 1), pre-exposure prophylaxis (n = 29), post-exposure prophylaxis (n = 3), HIV treatment (n = 20), sexually transmitted infection/hepatitis C virus testing/treatment (n = 12) and vaccination (n = 2). Fewer interventions were behavioural and psychosocial, including psychosocial support (n = 7), education (n = 11) and outreach (n = 3). Three took miscellaneous approaches. Few interventions primarily focused on mental health and substance use. Three addressed mental health: two using psychosocial strategies, one of which had a dual sexual health focus, and one assessing depression following HIV treatment initiation. Two addressed substance use, both with psychosocial approaches. Mental health outcome data (primary/secondary) were presented in nine interventions; substance use in five, mostly as secondary measures. Only one intervention reported outcomes spanning all three syndemic domains.

items.title: Smoking and dementia risk: an updated systematic review and meta-analysis of 61 prospective cohort studies and implications for tobacco control
items.originalTitle: Smoking and dementia risk: an updated systematic review and meta-analysis of 61 prospective cohort studies and implications for tobacco control
items.summary: Smoking has been identified as a modifiable dementia risk factor by three Lancet Commissions, yet dementia remains absent from most tobacco control strategies.
items.caution: Strongest kind of evidence — still check who took part.
items.abstract:
Background: Smoking has been identified as a modifiable dementia risk factor by three Lancet Commissions, yet dementia remains absent from most tobacco control strategies. The magnitude of the association across dementia subtypes, smoking categories, and population characteristics has not been comprehensively synthesised since 2015.

Methods: PubMed, Embase, CENTRAL, and PsycINFO were searched from January 2013 to 31 August 2026, updating the 2015 review, which contributed 34 studies. Random-effects meta-analyses (Restricted Maximum Likelihood (REML) with Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman adjustment) estimated pooled relative risks (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Subgroup analyses with tests for interaction and meta-regression examined effect modification by baseline age, ethnicity, follow-up duration, and adjustment for sex, education and Apolipoprotein E ε4 (APOE ε4) genotype. Risk of bias was assessed using Risk Of Bias In Non-randomized Studies of Exposures (ROBINS-E). Heterogeneity was assessed using Cochran's Q, I2 and τ2 and publication bias using funnel plots and Egger's test. Dose-response analysis of smoking and dementia risk was performed. Smoking population attributable fractions (PAF, unweighted and communality-weighted) for the risk of dementia were calculated. This study is registered with PROSPERO, CRD42025644539.

Findings: Sixty-one cohort studies (approximately 2.8 million participants) were included. Current smoking was associated with increased risk of all-cause dementia (RR 1.31 [95% CI 1.23-1.39]; number of studies (k) = 39), Alzheimer's disease (1.40 [1.08-1.80]; k = 15), and vascular dementia (1.52 [1.20-1.93]; k = 9). Former smoking was not associated with any outcome, and former smokers had a lower risk of all-cause dementia than current smokers (RR 0.81 [0.75-0.88]). I2 ranged from 0% to 80%. Egger's test suggested small-study effects only for current smoking and all-cause dementia (P = 0.09). The communality-weighted PAF for smoking and dementia was 2.2% (95% CI 1.7-2.8). Dementia risk increased with smoking intensity as the pooled RR was 1.16 (95% CI 1.09-1.23) at 10 cigarettes per day and rose to 1.34 (95% CI 1.18-1.51) at 20 cigarettes per day.

items.title: Neuropsychological evaluation and rehabilitation in multiple sclerosis (NEuRoMS): A mixed-methods, multi-centre feasibility randomised controlled trial
items.originalTitle: Neuropsychological evaluation and rehabilitation in multiple sclerosis (NEuRoMS): A mixed-methods, multi-centre feasibility randomised controlled trial
items.summary: Cognitive difficulties are common in people with multiple sclerosis (pwMS), yet access to neuropsychological rehabilitation is often limited or only provided to those with more severe impairments.
items.caution: Strongest kind of evidence — still check who took part.
items.source: Multiple sclerosis journal - experimental, translational and clinical
items.abstract:
Background: Cognitive difficulties are common in people with multiple sclerosis (pwMS), yet access to neuropsychological rehabilitation is often limited or only provided to those with more severe impairments. The NEuRoMS intervention provides brief, tailored neuropsychological rehabilitation for pwMS with mild-to-moderate cognitive difficulties.

Objectives: To evaluate feasibility and acceptability of the intervention and test procedures for a definitive trial.

Methods: A mixed-methods, multi-centre feasibility randomised controlled trial (RCT) was conducted. Feasibility outcomes were recruitment, retention, outcome completion, randomisation, intervention delivery and fidelity. Quantitative data were collected at baseline, 3- and 6-months, supplemented by interviews with pwMS and healthcare providers.

Results: Seventy-nine participants were randomised (mean age = 54.5 (SD = 11.5); 70% women) from three UK MS clinics. Most feasibility criteria were met: retention (>80%) and outcome-measure completion (81%-89%) were high, and trial procedures were acceptable. Intervention delivery was feasible and delivered as intended, but staffing-related recruitment challenges need addressing in future trials. Preliminary signal of efficacy was observed, with 3.42-point difference (effect size = 0.48) in the planned primary outcome (MS psychological impact) favouring the intervention, supported by qualitative evidence of sustained behaviour change.

Conclusion: The NEuRoMS intervention and trial procedures were feasible and acceptable, with early indication of efficacy. A definitive RCT is underway.Trial registration: ISRCTN11203922; https://doi.org/10.1186/ISRCTN11203922.
